rv.q: The script deftly unites moments broad and silly with elements wistful and serious within a simple structure.
There are big laughs and plenty of them, but they sit uneasily with the straighter strain of the story.
It proves fitfully enjoyable but is overshadowed by works that have ploughed the same theatrical furrow.
Yet it’s a baggy old evening, not quite a full-on gagfest, but too broad to sustain its aspirations to be something more substantial.
What's worse than a stage full of screaming children? A stage full of screaming adults pretending to be screaming children, that's what.
They blunder way outside their comfort zone with the child acting in the first half and again with the bittersweet dramedy stuff in the second, and it just doesn’t work.
By challenging themselves, pulling back (slightly) on the gags and injecting a sense of genuine pathos into their work, the creative team have really proven themselves top of the class.
The short answer is very well indeed, and the result would be even better if the director Kirsty Parkwe Ward's staging were more rigorous and the narrative more firmly grounded in logic.
Though it doesn't fully land, it's a good statement of intent, if not fully matched yet by its content.

cn.t: Mischief Theatre's classroom comedy divides critics, with some finding charm in its blend of broad humor and wistful nostalgia, while others deem it a grating departure from the company's signature theatrical chaos.
